articles.title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
articles.summary: OpenAI will cut frontier models off from the internet weeks after one of its engineers said that solution wouldn't work.
articles.full_text:
On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.

The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet.

Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies. “Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post .

OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet.

That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.

The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.

Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.” “In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with.

There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.” The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox?

No, it’s not,” he concluded.

Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox.

That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.

To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.” Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

articles.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
articles.summary: OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content "without risk of affecting external systems." OpenAI paused training its frontier […]
articles.full_text:
AI News OpenAI OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found.

AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found. by Emma Roth Oct 23, 2026, 9:11 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of The AI Superintelligence Slowdown see all updates Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents.

In a blog post on Friday , OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.” OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September , after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies , or swarm obscure websites .

On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.

Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection.

To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate.

One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache.

Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message.

Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.

OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication.

It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.” Related Sam Altman says OpenAI won’t go public until its models are safe One company is at the center of a wave of rogue AI attacks In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments.

It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects .

articles.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
articles.summary: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5.
articles.full_text:
23rd October 2026 - Link Blog Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro ( via ) Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026".

They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same).

The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5.

Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others.

Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58).

This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier.

I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace).

Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max.

articles.title: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
articles.summary: Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you'll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you're using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority, adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous […]
articles.full_text:
Tech AI News Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.

According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads. by Jess Weatherbed Oct 23, 2026, 4:52 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Jess Weatherbed is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture.

Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features.

The update, spotted by Android Authority , adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads.

While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.” That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.

Related Google dodges another breakup attempt Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.

This is what the policy says: “You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service.

For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.” “Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services.

For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.” If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.
